title: Tax the Super-Rich to Save Lives, Says Report
paragraphs: Taxing the world's richest people could help save tens of millions of lives in poorer countries, according to a new study published in the medical journal The Lancet.

The study was coordinated by Davide Rasella, a research professor at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal), and co-authored by economist Lucio Exposito of the University of East Anglia in the UK. The researchers analyzed data from 59 low- and lower-middle-income countries, home to 3.9 billion people, covering the period from 2002 to 2021.

The study comes at a time of sharp reductions in international aid. Official development assistance has fallen by nearly a quarter, and all major donor countries cut their aid budgets in 2024 and 2025. According to the researchers, if these cuts continue, they could lead to 7.6 million additional deaths by 2030, including 1.4 million children under the age of five. Exposito noted that donor countries are facing growing debt and are increasingly shifting money toward military spending.

To find possible solutions, the researchers modeled how different tax policies could replace the lost aid. The most effective option was a 3% annual tax on the wealth of billionaires, which they estimated could prevent up to 29.5 million deaths by 2030. Even a 1% tax could save around 15.1 million lives. Other options also had significant effects. A tax on financial transactions could prevent about 24.5 million deaths, while a global minimum tax on large multinational companies could prevent about 20.1 million.

The researchers pointed out that there are now more than 3,000 billionaires in the world, with a combined wealth of around $20.1 trillion. Rasella said that even modest policies to redistribute wealth could literally save tens of millions of lives in the coming years.

Some countries already tax wealth. Spain introduced a "solidarity" tax on large fortunes in 2022, while France has debated a similar measure, although its Senate rejected a recent proposal. Sweden, by contrast, abolished its wealth tax in 2007.
However, the researchers stressed that their figures are modeled estimates, not predictions of deaths that will definitely occur or be prevented.
